evidence: whole_row.py: _is_exempt (118-123) exempts a star whose node (Column parent or the star itself) is the argument of exp.Count, and any star with an exp.Exists ancestor. _expands_table (126-143) returns True only when a source in the star's SELECT scope is an exp.Table that _is_stored_relation (146-150); CTE and derived-table sources are Scope objects, not exp.Table, so a star over them returns False. Only a star inside the CTE or subquery that expands a stored table is refused, and that is outside the claim's 'names its own columns' qualifier. System catalogs: is_catalog_table (readonly.py:243-256) matches the catalog schema or name prefix per dialect, so _is_stored_relation is False and the star is allowed. Adversarial input traced: WITH c AS (SELECT a FROM t) SELECT * FROM c, which is allowed; SELECT * FROM information_schema.tables, which is allowed. The claim holds for each shape named.

assert_no_whole_row_select (whole_row.py:84-97) refuses only when first_sql_keyword is TABLE or _whole_row_star finds a non-exempt exp.Star. _whole_row_star (100-102) returns None at once if the statement has no exp.Star nodes. Crafted input `SELECT row_to_json(t) FROM t` parses to a Func over a Column, with no Star and no leading TABLE keyword, so no refusal is raised. The module docstring (32-34) also lists this as not covered. The release note matches the code.

configuration.md:32 states the claim. In whole_row.py, _whole_row_star (100-115) iterates every exp.Star in the whole statement, including those inside CTEs and subqueries, and refuses on _expands_table. For `WITH everything AS (SELECT * FROM users) SELECT id FROM everything`, the inner star's nearest Select is the CTE body, whose scope has selected_sources {users: exp.Table}. _is_stored_relation (146-150) is true for a non-catalog, non-function table, so it is refused. The outer query naming columns does not matter because the check is per star. Counter-input considered: a star in a CTE over a catalog, a table function or COUNT(*) is exempt, but the same doc sentence lists those as allowed, and they are not a star over a stored table. The module docstring (18-19) also says an inner star over a table is refused.

The doc rows are at read-only-safety.md:207 and 209 (the cited line 68 is elsewhere). readonly.py:45 defines first_sql_keyword(sql, dialect=None); dialect is the second positional parameter, and whole_row.py:90 calls it that way. It tokenizes with sqlglot (line 69), so comments attach to tokens and are not separate tokens. It skips L_PAREN tokens (74-75), uppercases the token text (76), and returns it if the token is VAR or a word whose KEYWORDS entry has the same token type (77-83). sqlglot's base tokenizer maps TABLE to TokenType.TABLE, so 'TABLE t', including after a leading comment, returns 'TABLE'. I did not run it, and I took the TABLE mapping from sqlglot's tokenizer rather than reading the installed copy.

readonly.py:571 signature _parse_statements(sql, dialect) positional, returns list[exp.Expression|None] (matches). But the 'could not parse SQL' prefix applies only to sqlglot ParseError/TokenError (readonly.py:585-586). Lexically ambiguous MySQL input raises UnsafeSqlError from _mysql_parse_sql with different messages (readonly.py:528 'MySQL backslash-escaped quotes are not allowed', :541, :544, :546, :552, :562), which propagate uncaught (not ParseError/TokenError) and do not begin with 'could not parse SQL'. Also empty SQL and dialect failures use other messages. Claim's message detail is wrong for ambiguous MySQL input. Callers (whole_row.py:92) only rely on UnsafeSqlError type, so impact is minor.

With dialect None or unlisted, the union applies (readonly.py:134-137), so all the named relations return True; with a specific dialect only that engine's catalogs plus information_schema count, consistent with 'such as'.

Installed sqlglot is 30.27.0 (dist-info METADATA), matching requirements.txt:105 pin. normalize_identifiers (optimizer/normalize_identifiers.py:24-101) walks the passed expression and calls dialect.normalize_identifier(node) on each Identifier, mutating nodes in place; it returns the same expression object (line 101), so discarding the return at whole_row.py:107 is fine for a parsed Expression statement. optimizer/scope.py defines class Scope (line 50) and def traverse_scope (line 672), so the import at whole_row.py:55 works.

Installed sqlglot optimizer/scope.py:439-464: selected_sources returns dict[str, (node, self.sources[name])], with name from self.references (node alias_or_name), and the second element typed exp.Table | Scope, so a Table for base tables and a Scope for CTEs/derived tables. Keys are the alias/name text, which equals Column.table text. whole_row.py:107 normalizes identifiers first, so case matches. Code at whole_row.py:134-139 uses entry[1] and the (node, source) unpack consistently. The 'something else' is a Scope, which is consistent with the claim. Semi/anti-join RHS names are skipped, which the code handles by treating a missing entry as expanding (line 135-136).

whole_row.py:108 builds {id(scope.expression): scope}; _expands_table (127-131) looks up id(star.find_ancestor(exp.Select)) and returns True (unsafe) when missing. In sqlglot scope.py, _traverse_scope yields scopes for Select (724-725, 793), for SetOperation operands via _traverse_set_operation, each branch scoped through _traverse_scope with Scope.branch, which sets expression=expression.unnest() (line 173), so the scope expression is the Select itself, not the Subquery wrapper. Projection/WHERE subqueries go through _traverse_subqueries (1017-1024), which branches the same way. CTEs via _traverse_ctes, DDL with Query body (739-744) and DML queries (767-787) are also scoped. Statements of other types (e.g. Command) yield no scopes (789-791, or [] at 705), so every star there hits the missing-scope branch and is treated as unsafe. The 'every Select' wording is true for ordinary queries; any Select outside a scope fails closed, as claimed. I read sqlglot from /opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.11.18/x64/lib/python3.11/site-packages (the installed dependency), not the repository view; I did not check that its version matches the project's pin.

whole_row.py:118-123 (_is_exempt) assumes: star is exp.Star, qualified star is exp.Column whose child is Star, COUNT arg parent is exp.Count, and EXISTS is an exp.Exists ancestor. whole_row.py:146-150 does check isinstance(table.this, exp.Func) inside _is_stored_relation, and _expands_table (141) first requires isinstance(source, exp.Table), so non-Table sources are skipped. The claim concerns sqlglot's parse trees, but no sqlglot source is in the views and I did not run a parse (e.g. parse_one('SELECT * FROM generate_series(1,3)').find(exp.Table).this). From memory, sqlglot's _parse_table_part tries _parse_function, so generate_series and pragma_table_info give Table.this as a Func. UNNEST, VALUES and LATERAL parse as exp.Unnest, exp.Values and exp.Lateral, not exp.Table, so the claim's UNNEST example is probably inaccurate. The repo's docs (read-only-safety.md:205) treat them as separate source kinds. The code is correct either way, but I could not confirm the library behaviour from available evidence.

In src/sqllens/safety/whole_row.py, _whole_row_star (100-115) checks every exp.Star in the statement via find_all, so position does not matter (projection, CTE, derived table, IN or scalar subquery, function argument). _expands_table (126-143) returns True when the star has no Select ancestor or its Select has no scope. This covers the hint's cases: DELETE/UPDATE ... RETURNING *, MERGE and star in window/ORDER BY contexts. A qualified star whose qualifier does not resolve is refused. Otherwise the star is refused when any selected source is a stored table or view. row_to_json(t.*) parses as Column(table=t, this=Star), so the Column parent is handled at lines 120 and 132. The only exemptions are COUNT, EXISTS, non-table sources and catalogs, and the docstring lists all of them. Absolute-claim input traced: SELECT row_to_json(t.*) FROM t, plus an IN subquery with SELECT * FROM t. Both reach _expands_table with a scope and a Table source, so both are refused. Scope-analysis exceptions propagate and the runner fails closed (170-188). I found no counterexample.

whole_row.py:126-150. _expands_table returns True only when a selected source is an exp.Table and _is_stored_relation holds. CTE and derived-table sources are Scope objects. VALUES and UNNEST are not exp.Table. A table-valued function is a Table whose .this is a Func, so _is_stored_relation returns False (line 148). Those sources are therefore allowed, as the docstring says. Every Select inside a CTE, derived table, LATERAL subquery or union branch is checked by the loop over all exp.Star nodes (line 109) against its own scope. A star with no resolvable scope returns True (lines 129-131), so a star the guard cannot place is refused. The inner star is refused unless it falls under the stated exemptions (EXISTS, COUNT, catalog), which the docstring lists separately. Hostile input I traced: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM u) x, and the same with LATERAL(SELECT * FROM u). The inner Select's scope has Table u as a source, so the star is refused. I read the code only and ran no queries.

whole_row.py:90 checks the TABLE shorthand only via first_sql_keyword (readonly.py:45-85), which returns only the leading keyword of the whole input. The loop at whole_row.py:92-97 skips None statements (empty statements, nothing to check) and otherwise inspects only stars (_whole_row_star). So a later statement such as `SELECT 1; TABLE users` is not caught by the TABLE check. It is refused only if sqlglot raises a ParseError on `TABLE users` (then _parse_statements raises UnsafeSqlError). If sqlglot parses it as a Command or similar with no Star, it passes, and the docstring 'every statement checked, whatever its kind' (line 87) would be false. The module docstring (lines 28-30) says sqlglot does not parse TABLE t as a SELECT, but does not say whether it raises. I did not run sqlglot.parse('SELECT 1; TABLE users', dialect='postgres'), and no test covers a non-leading TABLE (tests/unit/test_safety_whole_row.py:150 covers only leading). Missing evidence: that parse result.

whole_row.py:102-103: _whole_row_star returns None before normalize_identifiers (107) and traverse_scope (108) unless some star is non-exempt. These are the only calls to them in the module (grep of file read in full). Input traced: a statement with no stars (or only COUNT(*)/EXISTS stars) gives an empty/all-exempt find_all, so any() is False and it returns early. _is_exempt (118-123) uses only .parent, isinstance and find_ancestor, which cannot raise on any parent chain, and it runs only on stars, so a star-free statement never reaches it. first_sql_keyword and _parse_statements are separate and the docstring lists them separately (lines 36-41).

factory.py:85-101 builds engine runner, then RowCapRunner (91), ReadOnlyGuardRunner (94), RlsGuardRunner (101); WholeRowSelectGuardRunner is applied afterwards at 127, so it is outermost. It is the only construction site in src (grep). RlsGuardRunner.__init__ (safety/__init__.py:160) calls _relation_check_executor(inner), which unwraps only exact RlsGuardRunner/ReadOnlyGuardRunner/RowCapRunner (240) and runs on RlsGuardRunner's inner, which never contains the whole-row guard since that wraps outside. Hostile input considered: a second construction placing the guard beneath RLS; none exists in src. Fail-closed: whole_row.py:173-188 catches WholeRowSelectError, UnsafeSqlError and any other Exception, re-raising WholeRowSelectError, so the inner runner is not reached on any guard exception.

The same pattern is at limits.py:88 (RowCapRunner) and safety/__init__.py:129 and 209. The signature default is False (whole_row.py:171). readonly.py has no run_sql or forwarding at all, so the hint's mention of it does not change this.
